outputs.L1:
Recent studies of clustering in light nuclei with an initial energy above 1 A GeV in nuclear track emulsion are reviewed. The results of investigations into the fragmentation of relativistic $^9$Be nuclei in emulsion, accompanied by the production of He fragments, are presented. It is shown that the highly precise angular measurements provided by this technique play a crucial role in reconstructing the excitation spectrum of the $\alpha$-particle system. In peripheral interactions, $^9$Be nuclei dissociate almost entirely through the 0$^+$ and 2$^+$ states of the $^8$Be nucleus.

The results of investigations into the dissociation of a $^{14}$N nucleus with a momentum of 2.86 A GeV/c in emulsion are presented as an example of a more complicated system. The momentum and correlation characteristics of $\alpha$ particles for the $^{14}$N$\to3\alpha+X$ channel were considered in detail in both the laboratory system and the rest frame of the 3$\alpha$ particles.

The topology of charged fragments produced in the peripheral relativistic dissociation of radioactive $^8$B and $^7$Be nuclei in emulsion is also studied.

The text reviews recent research on clustering phenomena in light nuclei with initial energies exceeding 1 A GeV, studied using nuclear track emulsion. It presents findings from emulsion investigations of relativistic fragmentation of $^9$Be nuclei accompanied by the formation of helium fragments. The high-precision angular measurements made possible by this method are shown to be essential for reconstructing the excitation spectrum of the $\alpha$-particle system. In peripheral interactions, $^9$Be nuclei dissociate almost entirely via the 0$^+$ and 2$^+$ states of the $^8$Be nucleus.

As an example of a more complex nuclear system, results are also given for the emulsion study of $^{14}$N dissociation at a momentum of 2.86 A GeV/c. For the reaction channel $^{14}$N$\to3\alpha+X$, the momentum distributions and correlation properties of $\alpha$ particles were examined in detail both in the laboratory frame and in the rest frames of the three-$\alpha$ systems. In addition, the charge-fragment topology arising from peripheral relativistic dissociation of radioactive $^8$B and $^7$Be nuclei in emulsion is analyzed.
outputs.L3:
Recent studies have focused on the investigation of clustering phenomena in light nuclei at relativistic energies, particularly at initial energies above 1 A GeV. Nuclear track emulsion has proven to be an effective experimental technique for such work, because it provides high spatial resolution and allows detailed observation of the charged fragments produced in nuclear interactions. This makes it possible to analyze peripheral dissociation processes, in which the projectile nucleus breaks up while the target nucleus remains largely undisturbed, thereby preserving important information about the internal cluster structure of the projectile.

A significant part of these investigations concerns the fragmentation of relativistic \(^{9}\mathrm{Be}\) nuclei. In such reactions, helium fragments are frequently produced, and their angular distributions can be measured with high precision in nuclear emulsion. From these measurements, the invariant masses and excitation energies of systems composed of alpha particles can be reconstructed. This reconstruction provides access to the excitation spectrum of alpha-particle systems and helps clarify the role of cluster configurations in the structure of light nuclei.

The study of peripheral interactions of \(^{9}\mathrm{Be}\) has shown that its dissociation proceeds predominantly through the formation of unstable \(^{8}\mathrm{Be}\) states. In particular, almost all observed breakup events can be associated with the \(0^{+}\) ground state and the \(2^{+}\) excited state of the \(^{8}\mathrm{Be}\) nucleus. This result supports the interpretation of \(^{9}\mathrm{Be}\) as a system with a pronounced \(^{8}\mathrm{Be}+n\) cluster structure and demonstrates that relativistic fragmentation is a sensitive tool for studying such nuclear configurations.

Another important direction is the analysis of \(^{14}\mathrm{N}\) dissociation at a momentum of 2.86 A GeV/\(c\). This process has been studied through the channel  
\[
^{14}\mathrm{N}\rightarrow 3\alpha + X,
\]
where \(X\) denotes additional undetected or unmeasured fragments. Special attention is given to the momentum characteristics of the emitted alpha particles and to their correlation properties. By examining the angular and momentum distributions of the three-alpha system, researchers can identify possible intermediate cluster states and investigate whether the breakup proceeds through configurations related to \(^{12}\mathrm{C}\), including alpha-cluster states. Such studies contribute to a broader understanding of multi-alpha clustering in light nuclei.

The topology of charged fragments produced in the peripheral relativistic dissociation of radioactive \(^{8}\mathrm{B}\) and \(^{7}\mathrm{Be}\) nuclei has also been examined using nuclear track emulsion. These nuclei are of particular interest because of their weak binding and pronounced cluster features. The emulsion technique makes it possible to classify events according to the charges and emission angles of the fragments, thereby revealing the dominant breakup channels. For \(^{8}\mathrm{B}\), fragmentation patterns are especially relevant to understanding its proton-halo-like structure, while \(^{7}\mathrm{Be}\) dissociation provides insight into configurations such as \(^{3}\mathrm{He}+^{4}\mathrm{He}\).

Overall, these studies demonstrate the value of relativistic fragmentation in nuclear track emulsion for exploring cluster degrees of freedom in light nuclei. By analyzing fragment topologies, excitation spectra, and momentum correlations, researchers obtain detailed information about the internal structure of nuclei such as \(^{9}\mathrm{Be}\), \(^{14}\mathrm{N}\), \(^{8}\mathrm{B}\), and \(^{7}\mathrm{Be}\). The results confirm that clustering is a key feature of light nuclear systems and that peripheral dissociation at relativistic energies provides a powerful method for investigating it.
outputs.L4:
Studies of clustering in light nuclei at energies above 1 A GeV have shown that nuclear track emulsion remains a powerful method for investigating the relativistic fragmentation of light radioactive and stable nuclei. Owing to its excellent spatial resolution, this technique makes it possible to measure emission angles of relativistic fragments with high precision and, from these measurements, to reconstruct the invariant masses and excitation energies of fragment systems. Such information is especially valuable for identifying cluster configurations in nuclei, where the nucleus may behave as a loosely bound system of lighter substructures such as alpha particles, protons, or unstable intermediate nuclei.

In this work, nuclear track emulsion was used to study the peripheral fragmentation of several light nuclei, including \(^{9}\mathrm{Be}\), \(^{14}\mathrm{N}\), \(^{8}\mathrm{B}\), and \(^{7}\mathrm{Be}\), at energies exceeding 1 A GeV. Particular attention was paid to events in which the projectile nucleus dissociates with minimal disturbance from the target medium. These peripheral interactions, often called “white stars” when no target fragments or produced mesons are observed, provide especially clean information about the internal cluster structure of the projectile nucleus. Since the fragments retain nearly the velocity of the incoming nucleus, their momenta can be estimated from the projectile momentum per nucleon, while the measured emission angles determine the relative kinematics of the final-state fragments.

A central result was obtained for the dissociation of \(^{9}\mathrm{Be}\). This nucleus is known to have a pronounced cluster structure that can be approximated as a neutron coupled to an \(^{8}\mathrm{Be}\) core, with \(^{8}\mathrm{Be}\) itself rapidly decaying into two alpha particles. By measuring the opening angles between pairs of relativistic alpha particles produced in \(^{9}\mathrm{Be}\) fragmentation, the excitation energy of the two-alpha system was reconstructed. The analysis showed that peripheral \(^{9}\mathrm{Be}\) dissociation proceeds almost entirely through the \(0^+\) ground state and the \(2^+\) first excited state of \(^{8}\mathrm{Be}\). This confirms the dominant role of the \(^{8}\mathrm{Be}\) cluster component in the structure of \(^{9}\mathrm{Be}\).

The identification of these \(^{8}\mathrm{Be}\) states is significant because the ground state of \(^{8}\mathrm{Be}\) lies very close to the two-alpha threshold and has an extremely small decay energy, while the \(2^+\) state appears at higher excitation energy and produces alpha pairs with larger opening angles. The ability to distinguish these contributions using only angular measurements in emulsion demonstrates the precision of the method. It also shows that invariant-mass reconstruction in relativistic fragmentation can provide spectroscopic information comparable to that obtained by more conventional nuclear physics techniques.

The same experimental approach was extended to more complex systems such as \(^{14}\mathrm{N}\), \(^{8}\mathrm{B}\), and \(^{7}\mathrm{Be}\). These nuclei are of interest because their fragmentation channels may contain unstable intermediate states and cluster substructures involving alpha particles, deuterons, tritons, helions, and protons. For example, studies of neutron-deficient nuclei such as \(^{8}\mathrm{B}\) and \(^{7}\mathrm{Be}\) can reveal the role of loosely bound proton configurations and mirror or near-threshold cluster states. In heavier light nuclei such as \(^{14}\mathrm{N}\), the observation of multi-fragment final states provides information on how alpha clustering develops in systems with a larger number of nucleons.

Overall, these studies demonstrate that nuclear track emulsion, despite being a classical detector technique, remains highly effective for modern investigations of relativistic nuclear fragmentation. Its micrometric resolution enables accurate angular measurements, which in turn allow the reconstruction of excitation spectra of short-lived fragment systems. The results for \(^{9}\mathrm{Be}\), in particular, clearly show that peripheral dissociation is governed by the formation and decay of \(^{8}\mathrm{Be}\) in its \(0^+\) and \(2^+\) states. More broadly, the work confirms that emulsion measurements can reveal cluster degrees of freedom in light nuclei and can be applied to increasingly complex nuclear systems to study their internal structure.

Recent advances in high-energy physics have expanded our understanding of particles and forces at the GeV scale. A GeV, or giga-electronvolt, is a unit of energy commonly used to describe the masses and interactions of subatomic particles. The study of processes in this energy range is important because it helps scientists investigate the behavior of matter under extreme conditions.

The recent development of more precise detectors and particle accelerators has allowed researchers to collect better data and test theoretical models with greater accuracy. These experiments can reveal new details about protons, neutrons, mesons, and other particles. They also help bridge the gap between low-energy nuclear physics and the much higher energies explored in large collider experiments.

Overall, recent work involving GeV-scale physics continues to play a key role in modern science. The results may lead to deeper insights into the structure of the universe and the fundamental laws that govern it.

counterfactuals.prompt: Summarize research results on relativistic fragmentation of light nuclei above 1 A GeV in nuclear emulsion, with emphasis on alpha clustering in $^9$Be, $^{14}$N, $^8$B, and $^7$Be.
counterfactuals.output:
Research on relativistic fragmentation of light nuclei in nuclear emulsion at energies above about 1 A GeV shows that many light nuclei behave, in peripheral collisions, as preformed few-cluster systems. Nuclear emulsion is especially useful because it gives submicron spatial resolution and allows measurement of very small opening angles between relativistic fragments. In “white star” events — coherent dissociation with no produced mesons and no visible target-nucleus fragments — the projectile breaks up with minimal excitation, so the fragment topology reflects the cluster degrees of freedom already present in the projectile wave function.

A common analysis method assumes that relativistic fragments retain approximately the projectile velocity. Fragment momenta are then estimated from their emission angles and the projectile momentum per nucleon, allowing reconstruction of invariant masses and excitation energies such as

\[
Q = M^* - M_{\rm threshold}.
\]

Small values of \(Q\) identify decays through weakly bound cluster states such as \(^{8}\mathrm{Be}\), the Hoyle state of \(^{12}\mathrm{C}\), or near-threshold cluster configurations.

## General conclusions

Across nuclei such as \(^{7}\mathrm{Be}\), \(^{8}\mathrm{B}\), \(^{9}\mathrm{Be}\), and \(^{14}\mathrm{N}\), the emulsion data show:

- dominance of low-threshold cluster channels in peripheral fragmentation;
- frequent appearance of \(\alpha\)-particle substructures;
- preservation of projectile cluster configurations in relativistic dissociation;
- strong role of unstable intermediate nuclei, especially \(^{8}\mathrm{Be}\to 2\alpha\);
- usefulness of “white stars” as a clean probe of cluster components with minimal target disturbance.

The results support the idea that light nuclei at relativistic energies fragment mainly by rearrangement or liberation of preexisting clusters rather than by statistical evaporation.

---

## \(^{9}\mathrm{Be}\): two-\(\alpha\) clustering through \(^{8}\mathrm{Be}\)

The nucleus \(^{9}\mathrm{Be}\) is a classic example of a two-\(\alpha\) system with an additional neutron:

\[
^{9}\mathrm{Be} \approx \alpha + \alpha + n.
\]

Its neutron separation threshold is low, and the \(^{8}\mathrm{Be}+n\) configuration is strongly favored. In relativistic emulsion experiments, peripheral dissociation of \(^{9}\mathrm{Be}\) is dominated by the channel

\[
^{9}\mathrm{Be} \rightarrow 2\alpha + n,
\]

where the neutron is not directly observed in emulsion, but the two charged helium fragments are measured with high precision.

The key observable is the excitation energy of the two-\(\alpha\) system,

\[
Q_{2\alpha}=M^*(2\alpha)-2m_\alpha .
\]

A large fraction of \(^{9}\mathrm{Be}\to 2\alpha\) events have very small \(Q_{2\alpha}\), corresponding to decay through the ground state of \(^{8}\mathrm{Be}\):

\[
^{8}\mathrm{Be}_{\rm g.s.}\rightarrow \alpha+\alpha,
\]

whose energy above the \(2\alpha\) threshold is only about 92 keV. Events are also observed with larger \(Q_{2\alpha}\), associated with the first excited \(2^+\) state of \(^{8}\mathrm{Be}\) near 3 MeV.

Thus the emulsion results show that relativistic \(^{9}\mathrm{Be}\) dissociation proceeds largely as

\[
^{9}\mathrm{Be}\rightarrow ^8\mathrm{Be}+n\rightarrow 2\alpha+n.
\]

This is one of the clearest demonstrations, at relativistic energy, of a preformed \(2\alpha\) cluster core inside a light nucleus.

---

## \(^{14}\mathrm{N}\): multi-\(\alpha\) configurations and \(^{12}\mathrm{C}\)-like cores

For \(^{14}\mathrm{N}\), peripheral fragmentation frequently produces channels containing several helium fragments, especially topologies of the type

\[
^{14}\mathrm{N}\rightarrow 3\,\mathrm{He}+H,
\]

where the helium fragments are dominantly \(\alpha\) particles, though isotope identification in emulsion can be challenging without multiple scattering measurements. This charge topology corresponds naturally to configurations related to

\[
^{14}\mathrm{N}\approx ^{12}\mathrm{C}+d
\]

or

\[
^{14}\mathrm{N}\approx 3\alpha + d,
\]

with possible breakup into \(3\alpha\) plus a hydrogen isotope.

The important point is that \(^{14}\mathrm{N}\) fragmentation often reveals a three-\(\alpha\) subsystem, indicating that a \(^{12}\mathrm{C}\)-like cluster core is a significant component of the \(^{14}\mathrm{N}\) wave function. Invariant-mass analyses of three-\(\alpha\) systems are used to search for contributions from

\[
^{12}\mathrm{C}_{\rm g.s.},\quad ^{12}\mathrm{C}^*(7.65~\mathrm{MeV}),
\]

including the Hoyle state. The Hoyle state,

\[
^{12}\mathrm{C}_{0_2^+}\rightarrow 3\alpha,
\]

is of special interest because it represents a dilute three-\(\alpha\) configuration.

The \(^{14}\mathrm{N}\) data show that, in coherent dissociation, the nucleus often fragments by exposing an underlying \(3\alpha\) structure. Compared with pure \(^{12}\mathrm{C}\) fragmentation, the additional proton-neutron pair in \(^{14}\mathrm{N}\) can be viewed as a weakly coupled external cluster, often represented as a deuteron-like component.

A typical cluster interpretation is therefore:

\[
^{14}\mathrm{N}\rightarrow ^{12}\mathrm{C}+d
\rightarrow 3\alpha + d,
\]

or experimentally,

\[
^{14}\mathrm{N}\rightarrow 3\alpha + H + n,
\]

depending on the undetected neutron content.

---

## \(^{8}\mathrm{B}\): weakly bound proton plus \(^{7}\mathrm{Be}\) core

The proton-rich nucleus \(^{8}\mathrm{B}\) has a very low proton separation energy,

\[
S_p(^{8}\mathrm{B})\approx 137~\mathrm{keV},
\]

so it is naturally described as

\[
^{8}\mathrm{B}\approx ^7\mathrm{Be}+p.
\]

In relativistic emulsion experiments, the dominant peripheral white-star channel is

\[
^{8}\mathrm{B}\rightarrow ^7\mathrm{Be}+p.
\]

This confirms the weak binding of the external proton and the survival of a \(^{7}\mathrm{Be}\) core during gentle dissociation. The proton is emitted at very small angles, consistent with its low separation energy and halo-like or skin-like character.

Further breakup of the \(^{7}\mathrm{Be}\) core produces channels such as

\[
^{8}\mathrm{B}\rightarrow 2\,\mathrm{He}+H,
\]

reflecting the cluster structure of \(^{7}\mathrm{Be}\). Since

\[
^{7}\mathrm{Be}\approx \alpha + ^3\mathrm{He},
\]

the breakup of \(^{8}\mathrm{B}\) may be understood as

\[
^{8}\mathrm{B}\rightarrow p+\alpha+^3\mathrm{He}.
\]

Thus the relativistic fragmentation of \(^{8}\mathrm{B}\) has a two-level cluster character:

\[
^{8}\mathrm{B}\approx p+^{7}\mathrm{Be},
\]

with

\[
^{7}\mathrm{Be}\approx \alpha+^3\mathrm{He}.
\]

The emulsion data strongly support this picture. The lowest-threshold channel, \(^{7}\mathrm{Be}+p\), dominates in the most peripheral events, while more violent but still peripheral interactions reveal the \(\alpha+^3\mathrm{He}\) substructure of the \(^{7}\mathrm{Be}\) core.

---

## \(^{7}\mathrm{Be}\): \(\alpha+^{3}\mathrm{He}\) clustering

The nucleus \(^{7}\mathrm{Be}\) is a mirror partner of \(^{7}\mathrm{Li}\) and has a pronounced two-cluster structure:

\[
^{7}\mathrm{Be}\approx \alpha+^3\mathrm{He}.
\]

The threshold for breakup into \(\alpha+^3\mathrm{He}\) is relatively low, so the dominant coherent fragmentation channel in emulsion is

\[
^{7}\mathrm{Be}\rightarrow \mathrm{He}+\mathrm{He}.
\]

With isotope identification, this channel is interpreted mainly as

\[
^{7}\mathrm{Be}\rightarrow \alpha+^3\mathrm{He}.
\]

Other channels, such as

\[
^{7}\mathrm{Be}\rightarrow ^6\mathrm{Li}+p
\]

or

\[
^{7}\mathrm{Be}\rightarrow \alpha+d+p,
\]

can occur, but the two-helium topology is especially important because it directly exposes the \(\alpha+^3\mathrm{He}\) cluster configuration.

In white-star events, the dominance of the \(2\mathrm{He}\) final state indicates that \(^{7}\mathrm{Be}\) often dissociates by simple separation of its two main clusters, with little additional excitation. This makes \(^{7}\mathrm{Be}\) a compact but strongly clustered system.

---

## Comparative picture

The four nuclei illustrate a hierarchy of cluster structures:

\[
^{7}\mathrm{Be} \approx \alpha+^3\mathrm{He},
\]

\[
^{8}\mathrm{B} \approx p+^{7}\mathrm{Be}
          \approx p+\alpha+^3\mathrm{He},
\]

\[
^{9}\mathrm{Be} \approx n+^{8}\mathrm{Be}
          \approx n+\alpha+\alpha,
\]

\[
^{14}\mathrm{N} \approx d+^{12}\mathrm{C}
          \approx d+3\alpha.
\]

The common feature is the persistence of \(\alpha\)-cluster substructures during relativistic breakup. The most peripheral collisions tend to populate the lowest cluster thresholds, while excitation-energy spectra reveal intermediate resonant states such as \(^{8}\mathrm{Be}\) and possibly the Hoyle state of \(^{12}\mathrm{C}\).

## Main significance

The emulsion studies show that relativistic fragmentation is a powerful microscope for nuclear clustering. For the nuclei considered:

- \(^{9}\mathrm{Be}\) provides direct evidence for an \(^{8}\mathrm{Be}+n\), or \(2\alpha+n\), structure.
- \(^{14}\mathrm{N}\) often fragments through \(3\alpha+H\) channels, pointing to a \(^{12}\mathrm{C}\)-like three-\(\alpha\) core.
- \(^{8}\mathrm{B}\) shows a weakly bound external proton around a clustered \(^{7}\mathrm{Be}\) core.
- \(^{7}\mathrm{Be}\) is dominated by an \(\alpha+^3\mathrm{He}\) configuration.

Together, these results demonstrate that \(\alpha\) clustering remains a robust organizing principle in light nuclei even at relativistic projectile energies above 1 A GeV.

\[

where \(X\) denotes undetected or non-\(\alpha\) fragments. The observation of three-\(\alpha\) ensembles allows the search for intermediate cluster states, including possible \(^{8}\mathrm{Be}\) formation and \(3\alpha\) configurations related to excited states of \(^{12}\mathrm{C}\). Such channels are important for understanding how \(\alpha\)-cluster substructures appear in nuclei beyond the lightest systems.

Overall, the study demonstrates that relativistic dissociation in nuclear emulsion is a sensitive tool for investigating few-body cluster correlations, unstable intermediate nuclei, and the persistence of \(\alpha\)-cluster structure in light nuclei such as \(^{9}\mathrm{Be}\) and \(^{14}\mathrm{N}\).

counterfactuals.prompt: Produce a concise conference-style summary of experimental studies in nuclear track emulsion involving relativistic $^9$Be, $^{14}$N, $^8$B, and $^7$Be nuclei and their fragmentation channels.
counterfactuals.output:
### Conference-style summary

Nuclear track emulsion (NTE) studies of relativistic light nuclei provide a high-resolution method for investigating cluster degrees of freedom through peripheral fragmentation, especially in “white star” events, where the projectile dissociates without visible target fragments or produced mesons. Measurements of emission angles and charge topology allow reconstruction of invariant masses and identification of unstable cluster states such as \(^{8}\)Be.

#### \(^{9}\)Be fragmentation
Relativistic \(^{9}\)Be interactions show a pronounced two-\(\alpha\) topology, reflecting the well-known \(^{9}\)Be cluster structure
\[
^{9}\mathrm{Be} \rightarrow 2\alpha + n .
\]
The dominant coherent channel is
\[
^{9}\mathrm{Be} \rightarrow \alpha + \alpha ,
\]
with an undetected neutron. Angular correlations of the two \(\alpha\) particles reveal contributions from the \(^{8}\)Be ground state and low-lying excited states. The results confirm that \(^{9}\)Be behaves largely as a weakly bound \(^{8}\)Be–neutron system.

#### \(^{14}\)N fragmentation
Peripheral dissociation of relativistic \(^{14}\)N nuclei demonstrates strong multi-cluster features. Charge-topology measurements show frequent channels with total fragment charge \(Z=7\), especially configurations such as
\[
^{14}\mathrm{N} \rightarrow 3\,\mathrm{He} + \mathrm{H},
\]
consistent with an underlying \(3\alpha + p\) cluster component. The high probability of helium-rich final states indicates that \(\alpha\)-cluster correlations play an important role in the \(^{14}\)N ground-state structure and in its relativistic fragmentation.

#### \(^{8}\)B fragmentation
Studies of relativistic \(^{8}\)B are particularly sensitive to its proton-halo character. The leading peripheral channel is
\[
^{8}\mathrm{B} \rightarrow {}^{7}\mathrm{Be} + p ,
\]
with a narrow transverse-momentum distribution of the proton, supporting the picture of \(^{8}\)B as a loosely bound \(^{7}\)Be core plus an external proton. More violent breakup channels involving further fragmentation of the \(^{7}\)Be core, such as
\[
^{8}\mathrm{B} \rightarrow 2\,\mathrm{He} + \mathrm{H},
\]
also occur and provide information on the internal cluster structure of the core.

#### \(^{7}\)Be fragmentation
Relativistic \(^{7}\)Be fragmentation is dominated by the two-body cluster channel
\[
^{7}\mathrm{Be} \rightarrow {}^{4}\mathrm{He} + {}^{3}\mathrm{He},
\]
which directly reflects the \(\alpha + {}^{3}\)He structure of the nucleus. Events with two helium fragments are especially valuable because isotope identification through multiple scattering can separate \(^{3}\)He and \(^{4}\)He. The observed prevalence of this topology confirms the strong two-cluster nature of \(^{7}\)Be.

### Overall conclusion
Across \(^{9}\)Be, \(^{14}\)N, \(^{8}\)B, and \(^{7}\)Be, NTE measurements show that relativistic fragmentation proceeds largely through preformed cluster configurations. The dominant channels—\(^{9}\)Be \(\rightarrow 2\alpha+n\), \(^{14}\)N \(\rightarrow 3\mathrm{He}+\mathrm{H}\), \(^{8}\)B \(\rightarrow {}^{7}\)Be+\(p\), and \(^{7}\)Be \(\rightarrow {}^{4}\)He+\(^{3}\)He—demonstrate the sensitivity of emulsion techniques to \(\alpha\)-clustering, core-plus-nucleon structures, and halo degrees of freedom in light nuclei.
